new_statements.translation: Stress always occurs on the last syllable of the word, in disyllabic as well as trisyllabic and polysyllabic words in general, including derived words, as shown in examples (4), (5), (6) and (7) respectively. (4) a) [pa.ˈma] 'Pama' b) [ta.ˈmɯ] 'cigarette, tobacco' ... (6) a) [ta.gan.ta.ˈga] 'butterfly' ... (7) i) [ɯ.ˈdɔ] 'Go!' j) [ɯ.dɔ.ˈlɯ] 'He went away' k) [ɯ.dɔ.lɯŋ.ˈmɔ] 'They went away'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of every word, regardless of syllable weight or structure and regardless of affixation (suffixes carry the stress with them). Alves 2010 (same author, pp. 29-33, 39) adds the caveat that final prominence is perceived but instrumental cues (vowel quality, VOT, F0, duration) do not distinguish a stressed syllable beyond consistent final lengthening; Souza 2010 (pp. 19-21) and Souza 1988 (p. 11) independently describe the Laranjal dialect with the same final pattern.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source; Alves 2010 (p. 33) tested for foot-based alternation in CVCVCVCV words and found no convergent cue pattern.
new_statements.exceptions: Alves 2017: none. Souza 2010 (pp. 19-21): words ending in V + high V vary between final stress (careful speech) and stress on the preceding vowel with a monosyllabic reading ([po'u] ~ ['pou] 'small peccary'); in trisyllables only when the penult consonant is a liquid ([kaɾe'i] ~ [ka'ɾei]); within sentences stress can move off the final syllable ([iʧiɡu'ɾu] 'his urine', [u'ɾɔ] 'I' stressed on the third and second syllable from the right in (54)). Souza 1988 (p. 11): a rare penult type (S)'S S, only the word for 'aqui' exclusively.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; Souza 2010 states the rule for words pronounced in isolation (list/citation forms) and notes phrase-internal shifts; Alves 2010 could not separate prominence from phrase-final lengthening.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Pará Arára (para1310, ISO aap). Alves 2010/2013/2017 describe mainly the dialect of the Iriri / Cachoeira Seca do Iriri village (TI Cachoeira Seca), with notes on the Laranjal ('dialeto Arara') variety; Souza 1988/2010 and S. Souza 2010 describe the Laranjal village dialect (TI Arara). Alves 2010 says the two dialects are phonologically very similar and both sets of sources report final stress. Glottolog gives no dialect-level glottocodes. Nimuendajú's Parirí (1914) is an older variety listed under the same glottocode.

sources.note: Sec. 2.6 'Nota sobre o acento', p. 42: stress always on the last syllable of the word, in di-, tri- and polysyllables and in derived words (examples (4)-(7)); p. 38: the GV vs VV contrast is carried by stress, which 'recai sempre sobre a última sílaba da palavra'. No secondary stress, no exceptions mentioned. Data mainly from the Iriri (Cachoeira Seca) dialect.

sources.citation: Ferreira Alves, Ana Carolina. 2010. Phonological Aspects of Arara (Carib, Brazil). MA thesis, Radboud Universiteit Nijmegen, 43 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Sec. 4 'Stress', pp. 29-33: prominence is perceived on the last syllable of words regardless of syllable structure; affixes are stress-neutral (final prominence in underived and derived words); but instrumental measurements of vowel quality, VOT, F0 and duration 'suggest the absence of phonetic stress in Arara' (p. 33); conclusion p. 39: 'no strong evidence of stress pattern', only the final syllable is consistently longer (prominence vs phrase-final lengthening undecided). Cachoeira Seca variety mainly.

sources.note: Sec. 3.1.3 'Stress', pp. 19-21 (PDF pp. 32-33): in isolation primary stress 'preferentially falls on the last syllable of the word'; when a word ends in V + [+high] V the stress may shift to the preceding vowel (disyllabic careful-speech vs monosyllabic normal-speech realization, e.g. [po'u] ~ ['pou]); not in trisyllables unless the penult consonant is a liquid; within sentences stress can move off the final syllable (ex. (54)). Laranjal dialect.
